cards.title: Bubble Sort
cards.teaser: Bubble sort repeatedly walks the array, swapping adjacent elements that are out of order. The largest unsorted element 'bubbles' to the end after each pass. It's O(n²) in all cases and never used in production — but its simplicity makes it ideal for learning.

runs.text: Bubble sort is the simplest comparison-based sorting algorithm. It makes repeated passes over the array. In each pass, adjacent elements are compared and swapped if the left one is larger. After the first pass, the largest element has bubbled to the last position. After the second pass, the second-largest is in place. After
passes, the array is sorted.

explanation.code:
def bubble_sort(arr: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    n = len(arr)
    for i in range(n - 1):           # n-1 passes
        swapped = False
        for j in range(n - 1 - i):   # shrink window each pass
            if arr[j] > arr[j + 1]:
                arr[j], arr[j + 1] = arr[j + 1], arr[j]
                swapped = True
        if not swapped:               # early exit if already sorted
            break
    return arr

print(bubble_sort([5, 3, 8, 1, 2]))  # [1, 2, 3, 5, 8]

runs.text: The
swapped

flag is the one practical optimization: if a full pass produces no swaps, the array is already sorted and we can exit early. This gives O(n) best-case performance on already-sorted input, though worst-case and average case remain O(n²).

items.text: average and worst case; O(n) best case with the early-exit optimization.
— sorts in place with only a handful of extra variables.
yes — equal elements are never swapped, preserving original order.

runs.text: Never use bubble sort on real data. Even on 10,000 elements it is orders of magnitude slower than Python's built-in sorted(). Its only value is as a teaching tool — the inner-loop structure illustrates the O(n²) problem that better algorithms solve.

Bubble sort walks the array over and over, swapping neighbors that are in the wrong order. After each walk, the biggest remaining element has drifted to its final spot. It's simple to understand but painfully slow — O(n²) — and exists only as a classroom example of what not to do in production.

cards.title: Selection Sort
cards.teaser: Selection sort finds the minimum element in the unsorted portion and swaps it to the front. It always runs O(n²) comparisons — the early-exit optimization that helps bubble sort doesn't apply — but it performs at most O(n) swaps, making it good when writes are expensive.

runs.text: Selection sort divides the array into a sorted left portion and an unsorted right portion. In each pass, it scans the entire unsorted portion to find the minimum element, then swaps it into the next sorted position. After
passes, the array is sorted.

explanation.code:
def selection_sort(arr: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    n = len(arr)
    for i in range(n - 1):
        min_idx = i
        for j in range(i + 1, n):      # find minimum in unsorted portion
            if arr[j] < arr[min_idx]:
                min_idx = j
        if min_idx != i:               # swap only if needed
            arr[i], arr[min_idx] = arr[min_idx], arr[i]
    return arr

print(selection_sort([64, 25, 12, 22, 11]))  # [11, 12, 22, 25, 64]

runs.text: Selection sort makes exactly
comparisons regardless of input order — there is no early-exit shortcut. However, it performs at most
swaps (one per pass), compared to bubble sort's potential O(n²) swaps. This makes it preferable when the cost of writing data to memory or disk is high relative to the cost of reading.

items.text: — the swap can move an equal element past another.
— at most one swap per pass.

runs.text: The low swap count makes selection sort interesting in specific embedded contexts where flash memory has write-cycle limits. In general software, it remains a teaching algorithm — use sorted() or heapq in production.

Selection sort repeatedly scans the unsorted part, picks the smallest element, and moves it to the front. It's O(n²) with no shortcut, but it swaps at most n times — useful if writes are expensive. In practice, just use Python's built-in sort.

cards.title: Insertion Sort
cards.teaser: Insertion sort builds a sorted sequence one element at a time by inserting each new element into its correct position among the already-sorted elements. It's O(n²) worst case but O(n) on nearly-sorted data, making it the go-to for small arrays and the final step inside Timsort.

runs.text: Insertion sort processes elements left to right. For each element at position
i

, it shifts all larger sorted elements one position to the right to create a gap, then inserts the current element into that gap. The analogy is sorting a hand of playing cards: you pick up each card and slot it into the correct place among the cards you're already holding.
On an already-sorted array, the inner
while

loop never executes — each element is already in place, so insertion sort runs in O(n) time. On a nearly-sorted array (one or two elements out of place), it is extremely fast. This adaptive behavior is why Timsort uses insertion sort for small subarrays.

items.text: worst/average; O(n) best case on sorted or nearly-sorted input.
— equal elements retain original relative order.
— faster when input is partially sorted.

runs.text: The standard rule of thumb: for n ≤ 32, insertion sort beats merge sort and quicksort in practice due to low constant factors and cache-friendly sequential access. CPython's Timsort and many C++ standard library implementations use this threshold.

Insertion sort picks each element and slides it leftward into its correct spot among the elements already sorted. It's like sorting playing cards in your hand. Worst case is O(n²), but on nearly-sorted data it's O(n) — that adaptive behavior is why it's used inside Python's own sort algorithm.

cards.title: Merge Sort
cards.teaser: Merge sort is a divide-and-conquer algorithm that splits the array in half, recursively sorts each half, then merges the two sorted halves. It is always O(n log n) and stable, but requires O(n) extra memory — a fair trade when stability and predictable performance matter.

runs.text: Merge sort splits the input into halves until each piece has one element (trivially sorted), then merges adjacent pieces in order. The merge step is where the real work happens: two sorted lists can be merged into one sorted list in O(n) by repeatedly picking the smaller of the two front elements.

The complexity argument: the array is halved at each level, giving O(log n) levels of recursion. At each level, the total work merging all the pieces is O(n). Total: O(n log n), and this bound holds regardless of input order — there is no bad case for merge sort.
The cost is memory: each merge creates a new list, so O(n) extra space is used at any one time. An in-place merge sort exists but is significantly more complex and slower in practice.

items.text: — the <= in the merge step preserves order of equal elements.

runs.text: Merge sort's guaranteed O(n log n) and stability make it the preferred sort for linked lists (no random access needed) and external sorting (data too large to fit in RAM), where data arrives in sequential chunks.

Merge sort splits the array in half repeatedly until each piece has one element, then merges pairs of sorted pieces back together. Merging two sorted lists is easy: just compare the fronts and take the smaller one. The split gives O(log n) levels, each level does O(n) work, so total time is always O(n log n).

cards.title: Quicksort
cards.teaser: Quicksort picks a pivot, partitions the array into elements less than and greater than the pivot, then recursively sorts each partition. Average case is O(n log n) and in-place, but a bad pivot choice can degrade to O(n²) — randomized pivot selection prevents this in practice.

runs.text: Quicksort is the most widely used general-purpose sort in practice. Its inner loop is tight and cache-friendly. The algorithm works in three steps: choose a
pivot
element,
partition
the array so that all elements less than the pivot are on its left and all greater are on its right, then
recurse
on the two partitions.

explanation.code:
import random

def quicksort(arr: list[int], lo: int = 0, hi: int | None = None) -> list[int]:
    if hi is None:
        hi = len(arr) - 1
    if lo < hi:
        pivot_idx = _partition(arr, lo, hi)
        quicksort(arr, lo, pivot_idx - 1)
        quicksort(arr, pivot_idx + 1, hi)
    return arr

def _partition(arr: list[int], lo: int, hi: int) -> int:
    # Randomized pivot: swap a random element to the end
    rand_idx = random.randint(lo, hi)
    arr[rand_idx], arr[hi] = arr[hi], arr[rand_idx]
    pivot = arr[hi]
    i = lo - 1
    for j in range(lo, hi):
        if arr[j] <= pivot:
            i += 1
            arr[i], arr[j] = arr[j], arr[i]
    arr[i + 1], arr[hi] = arr[hi], arr[i + 1]
    return i + 1

print(quicksort([10, 7, 8, 9, 1, 5]))  # [1, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10]

runs.text: The worst case arises when the pivot is always the smallest or largest element — the partition is maximally unbalanced, producing subarrays of size 0 and n−1. This gives O(n²) time and O(n) stack depth, which is exactly what happens with a fixed last-element pivot on an already-sorted array. Randomized pivot selection reduces this to an astronomically unlikely event.

items.text: average; O(n²) worst case (prevented by randomization).
average stack depth; O(n) worst case.
— the partition swaps may reorder equal elements.

runs.text: Python's sorted() / list.sort() does not use quicksort — it uses Timsort. C's qsort() and C++'s std::sort() use introsort (quicksort + heapsort fallback) to guarantee O(n log n) worst case while keeping quicksort's speed in practice.

Quicksort picks a pivot, rearranges the array so smaller elements go left and larger go right, then sorts each side the same way. With a random pivot it's O(n log n) in practice, in-place, and very fast. The risk is a bad pivot — always sorted or always worst-split — which makes it O(n²), which randomization makes almost impossible.

cards.title: Heapsort
cards.teaser: Heapsort builds a max-heap from the array, then repeatedly extracts the maximum to sort in-place. It achieves O(n log n) in all cases with O(1) extra space — better guarantees than quicksort, but slower in practice due to poor cache behavior.

runs.text: Heapsort runs in two phases. First, it transforms the array into a
max-heap

in O(n) time using the heapify-down trick. Second, it repeatedly swaps the root (the maximum) with the last element of the heap, shrinks the heap by one, and sifts the new root down to restore the heap property. Each extraction takes O(log n); doing it n times gives O(n log n) total.

Heapsort's worst-case O(n log n) and O(1) space make it theoretically superior to quicksort. In practice, quicksort is typically faster because heapsort's access pattern jumps around the array non-sequentially, thrashing CPU caches. Introsort (used by C++ std::sort) runs quicksort and only falls back to heapsort when recursion depth exceeds O(log n), getting the best of both.

Python's heapq module implements a min-heap. To replicate heapsort behavior, use heapq.heapify() + repeated heapq.heappop() — but this allocates O(n) space. The in-place version above is more efficient but requires implementing sift_down manually.

Heapsort turns the array into a max-heap (where each parent is larger than its children), then repeatedly pulls the largest element from the top and places it at the end. It's O(n log n) with no extra memory — no bad inputs either. The catch: cache performance is poor, so quicksort is faster in practice despite heapsort's stronger theoretical guarantees.

cards.title: Timsort (Python's Built-in Sort)
cards.teaser: Timsort is Python's sorting algorithm, powering sorted() and list.sort(). It detects natural runs of already-ordered data, extends short runs with insertion sort, then merges runs with merge sort's merge step. It's O(n log n) worst case and O(n) on already-sorted data.

runs.text: Timsort was designed by Tim Peters in 2002, specifically for Python, to be fast on the kinds of data that appear in real programs — partially sorted, containing runs, or with repeated values. It is now also used in Java's
Arrays.sort()
for objects and V8's
Array.prototype.sort()
The algorithm works as follows:

items.text: — consecutive ascending (or descending, then reversed) sequences in the input.
— runs shorter than the minrun threshold (32–64 elements) are extended to minrun length using insertion sort.
— runs are pushed onto a stack and merged according to invariants that keep the stack balanced, similar to merge sort.
— during a merge, if one run is consistently winning comparisons, Timsort switches to binary search ("galloping") to skip large swaths rather than comparing element-by-element.

explanation.code:
# Python's sorted() and list.sort() both use Timsort under the hood
data = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6, 5, 3, 5]

# Returns a new sorted list
sorted_data = sorted(data)

# Sorts in place (more efficient — no copy)
data.sort()

# Both are O(n log n) worst case, O(n) on already-sorted input
already_sorted = list(range(10_000))
data2 = sorted(already_sorted)  # very fast: O(n), just one run

items.text: worst case; O(n) best case on sorted input.
— merge buffers, but only half the input size at any time.

runs.text: Always prefer Python's built-in sorted() or list.sort() over any hand-written sort. Timsort is implemented in C, extensively tuned, and exploits real-world data patterns that academic sorting algorithms ignore.

Timsort is the sort Python actually uses. It looks for stretches of already-sorted data (runs), fills in short ones with insertion sort, then merges everything with merge sort's merge step. On real-world data that's often partially ordered, it's extremely fast. On totally random data it falls back to O(n log n). It's stable, and you should always just use sorted() or list.sort() — they call Timsort in C.

cards.title: Counting Sort
cards.teaser: Counting sort runs in O(n + k) time by counting how many times each value appears, then reconstructing the sorted array from those counts. It's not a comparison sort — it exploits the fact that values are bounded integers in a known range [0, k).

runs.text: Comparison-based sorts cannot do better than O(n log n) because they rely on pairwise comparisons, and information theory proves you need at least log₂(n!) comparisons to distinguish all n! orderings. Counting sort sidesteps this lower bound by never comparing elements — it just counts occurrences.

explanation.code:
def counting_sort(arr: list[int], k: int) -> list[int]:
    """Sort arr where all values are in [0, k)."""
    counts = [0] * k
    for val in arr:
        counts[val] += 1           # tally each value

    result: list[int] = []
    for val, count in enumerate(counts):
        result.extend([val] * count)   # reconstruct in order
    return result

print(counting_sort([4, 2, 2, 8, 3, 3, 1], k=9))  # [1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 8]

# Stable variant: cumulative counts give insertion positions
def counting_sort_stable(arr: list[int], k: int) -> list[int]:
    counts = [0] * k
    for val in arr:
        counts[val] += 1
    for i in range(1, k):
        counts[i] += counts[i - 1]   # prefix sums → end positions
    output = [0] * len(arr)
    for val in reversed(arr):        # reversed for stability
        counts[val] -= 1
        output[counts[val]] = val
    return output

runs.text: The key parameters:
n
is the number of elements,
k
is the range of values. When
k
is O(n), counting sort is O(n) — faster than any comparison sort. When
k
is much larger than
n
(e.g., sorting 100 values from range [0, 10⁹]), the large count array wastes memory and time.

items.text: — for the count array and output.
— values must map to array indices.

runs.text: Counting sort is a subroutine inside radix sort. It is also used directly for sorting scores (0–100), ages, character frequencies in strings, and histogram-based operations.

Counting sort doesn't compare elements at all — it counts how many times each value appears, then rebuilds the array by listing each value its count number of times. This makes it O(n + k) where k is the value range. When k is small (like sorting exam scores 0–100), it's faster than any comparison-based sort.

cards.title: Radix Sort
cards.teaser: Radix sort sorts integers digit by digit, from least significant to most significant, using a stable sort (typically counting sort) at each digit position. It runs in O(d·n) time where d is the number of digits — effectively O(n) for fixed-width integers.

runs.text: Radix sort exploits the structure of integers (or fixed-length strings). Instead of comparing whole values, it sorts by one digit (or character) at a time. The crucial requirement: the per-digit sort must be
stable
— elements with the same digit at the current position must retain their order from the previous pass. This is why counting sort is used as the inner subroutine.

explanation.code:
def counting_sort_by_digit(arr: list[int], exp: int) -> list[int]:
    """Stable sort by the digit at position exp (1, 10, 100, ...)."""
    n = len(arr)
    output = [0] * n
    counts = [0] * 10

    for val in arr:
        digit = (val // exp) % 10
        counts[digit] += 1
    for i in range(1, 10):
        counts[i] += counts[i - 1]   # prefix sums
    for val in reversed(arr):         # reversed for stability
        digit = (val // exp) % 10
        counts[digit] -= 1
        output[counts[digit]] = val
    return output

def radix_sort(arr: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    max_val = max(arr)
    exp = 1
    while max_val // exp > 0:
        arr = counting_sort_by_digit(arr, exp)
        exp *= 10
    return arr

print(radix_sort([170, 45, 75, 90, 802, 24, 2, 66]))  # [2, 24, 45, 66, 75, 90, 170, 802]

runs.text: With
d
digit positions and
n

elements, radix sort runs in O(d · n). For 32-bit integers with base 256, d = 4 passes and k = 256 — so in practice it is O(4n) = O(n). This beats O(n log n) for large n, but requires O(n) extra space for each counting sort pass.

items.text: Constraint: keys must have fixed-width digit representation
— works for integers, fixed-length strings, IP addresses.

runs.text: Radix sort is used in database engines and network routers for sorting large numbers of fixed-width keys (IP addresses, port numbers, timestamps) where the constant factor of O(n log n) comparison sorts becomes meaningful at billions of rows.

Radix sort sorts numbers digit by digit — first by the ones place, then tens, then hundreds, and so on — using a stable sort each time. Because each pass is stable, the relative order from previous passes is preserved, and after all digit positions are processed, the array is fully sorted. It's O(d·n), which is effectively O(n) for fixed-size integers.

cards.title: Stable vs. Unstable Sorts
cards.teaser: A stable sort preserves the original order of elements that compare as equal. An unstable sort may reorder them. Stability matters whenever you sort by multiple keys — sort by secondary key first, then primary key with a stable sort, and the combined order is correct.

runs.text: Two elements are "equal" with respect to the sort key when the comparison function returns 0 (or
False
for both
a < b
and
b < a
stable sort
guarantees that among equal elements, the one that appeared earlier in the input appears earlier in the output.
A concrete example: sorting a list of employees first by department, then by name within each department.

explanation.code:
employees = [
    {"name": "Alice",   "dept": "Engineering"},
    {"name": "Bob",     "dept": "Marketing"},
    {"name": "Charlie", "dept": "Engineering"},
    {"name": "Diana",   "dept": "Marketing"},
]

# Multi-key sort using Python's stable sort:
# Step 1: sort by secondary key (name)
employees.sort(key=lambda e: e["name"])
# Result: Alice, Bob, Charlie, Diana

# Step 2: sort by primary key (dept) — STABLE preserves name order within dept
employees.sort(key=lambda e: e["dept"])
# Result: Alice (Eng), Charlie (Eng), Bob (Mkt), Diana (Mkt)
# Within each dept, alphabetical name order is preserved from step 1

# Equivalent one-step sort using tuple key:
employees.sort(key=lambda e: (e["dept"], e["name"]))

runs.text: Stable algorithms: merge sort, Timsort, counting sort (stable variant), insertion sort, bubble sort. Unstable: quicksort, heapsort, selection sort. Python's
sorted()
and
list.sort()
are always stable — this is guaranteed by the language spec.

Any unstable sort can be made stable by augmenting each element with its original index: sort by (key, original_index). This guarantees a tie-break that preserves input order. Python's sort does this internally.

A stable sort keeps equal elements in their original order relative to each other. This matters when you sort by multiple criteria: sort by secondary key first, then by primary key using a stable sort — the secondary ordering is preserved within each primary group. Python's sort is always stable, which is why the two-pass technique works.

cards.title: In-Place vs. Out-of-Place Sorting
cards.teaser: An in-place sort rearranges elements within the original array using O(1) extra space. An out-of-place sort allocates a separate output array. In-place saves memory but is harder to implement correctly; out-of-place is simpler and often faster due to better access patterns.

runs.text: An
in-place sort
modifies the input array directly, using only O(1) auxiliary space beyond the input itself (stack frames for recursion are usually not counted, or are bounded). An
out-of-place sort
builds a new sorted array, leaving the original intact.

explanation.code:
# In-place: modifies original array
def in_place_example(arr: list[int]) -> None:
    arr.sort()          # Timsort, in-place
    # arr is now sorted; original reference is modified

# Out-of-place: leaves original intact, returns new list
def out_of_place_example(arr: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    return sorted(arr)  # Timsort, out-of-place copy

original = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5]
copy = out_of_place_example(original)
print(original)  # [3, 1, 4, 1, 5] — unchanged
print(copy)      # [1, 1, 3, 4, 5]

in_place_example(original)
print(original)  # [1, 1, 3, 4, 5] — modified

runs.text: The trade-offs:

items.text: (quicksort, heapsort, insertion sort): saves memory, no copy overhead, but the original data is destroyed. Algorithms are often more complex.
(merge sort, counting sort, radix sort): original is preserved, easier to implement correctly, but uses O(n) extra memory.
is in-place; sorted() is out-of-place and returns a new list.

runs.text: In Python, list.sort() uses O(n/2) temporary space internally during merges — it is not truly O(1). The distinction matters more in languages like C where you control memory explicitly, or in embedded systems with constrained RAM.

In-place sorting rearranges the original array without extra memory (quicksort, heapsort). Out-of-place sorting creates a fresh sorted copy (merge sort, sorted()). Use list.sort() when you want in-place and don't need the original; use sorted() when you want to keep the original unchanged. Both use Timsort internally — the difference is only whether a copy is made.

cards.title: Sort Key Functions in Python
cards.teaser: Python's sorted() and list.sort() accept a key= parameter: a function applied to each element before comparison. This avoids modifying the data, allows complex multi-field sorting, and is significantly faster than a custom comparison function via functools.cmp_to_key.

runs.text: The
key=

parameter implements the Schwartzian transform: Python calls the key function once per element, sorts by the resulting values, then returns the elements in that order. The original elements are never mutated — only the sort keys are compared.

explanation.code:
from operator import attrgetter, itemgetter
from functools import cmp_to_key

words = ["banana", "Apple", "cherry", "date"]

# Case-insensitive sort
print(sorted(words, key=str.lower))          # ['Apple', 'banana', 'cherry', 'date']

# Sort by length, then alphabetically
print(sorted(words, key=lambda w: (len(w), w.lower())))
# ['date', 'Apple', 'banana', 'cherry']

# Sort list of dicts by a field
records = [{"name": "Charlie", "age": 30}, {"name": "Alice", "age": 25}]
print(sorted(records, key=itemgetter("age")))  # Alice first

# Sort objects by attribute
class Person:
    def __init__(self, name: str, age: int):
        self.name = name
        self.age = age

people = [Person("Zoe", 22), Person("Alice", 30)]
people.sort(key=attrgetter("age"))           # Zoe first

# Descending sort: negate the key or use reverse=True
nums = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9]
print(sorted(nums, key=lambda x: -x))        # [9, 5, 4, 3, 1, 1]
print(sorted(nums, reverse=True))             # same result

runs.text: Key functions are called exactly once per element before sorting begins. This is far more efficient than
cmp_to_key
(which wraps a comparison function), because the key is computed O(n) times total rather than O(n log n) times during comparisons.

items.text: — faster than a lambda for dict field or tuple index access.
— faster than a lambda for object attribute access; supports dotted names like 'address.city'.
— return a tuple from the key function to sort by multiple fields: primary, secondary, tertiary.
— reverses the entire sort; combine with a tuple key for mixed ascending/descending by negating numeric fields.

runs.text: For strings that need locale-aware sorting (accented characters, case folding by locale), use locale.strxfrm as the key function or the third-party natsort library. Python's default string comparison is Unicode code point order, which is not always alphabetical for non-ASCII text.

The key= parameter in sorted() lets you tell Python what to compare. Pass a function and Python calls it once per element, sorts by those results, and returns the original elements in order. Use a lambda for quick transforms, operator.itemgetter for dict fields, operator.attrgetter for object attributes. Return a tuple to sort by multiple fields at once.
